1.title: The Six Scenarios Worked End to End
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: The Six Scenarios Worked End to End. This module covers the six scenarios worked end to end. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. For each of the six scenarios: the requirement, the design decisions that the exam tests, and the traps. How the ten decision rules show up inside each scenario. Which module to reread when a scenario feels weak.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply. The solution architect meets the topic of this module. Your job: decide, step by step, which design choice fits.

1.title: Scenario 1: Customer Support Resolution Agent
1.text: Scenario one: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Requirement: an Agent S D K (software development kit) agent with M C P (Model Context Protocol) tools (get customer, lookup order, process refund, escalate to human); eighty percent plus first-contact resolution; knows when to escalate.

1.title: Scenario 1: Customer Support Resolution Agent, continued
1.text: Scenario one: Customer Support Resolution Agent, continued. Loop control. Best answer: Continue on tool use, stop on end turn. Module: one. Verify the customer before money moves. Best answer: Programmatic prerequisite gate, not a prompt reminder. Module: three. Refund limit. Best answer: Hook that blocks above the limit and redirects to escalation. Module: three. Confusion between similar tools. Best answer: Better tool descriptions first. Module: five. Tool failures. Best answer: Structured errors with category and retryable flag; business errors explain themselves. Module: five. Mixed-up facts in long chats. Best answer: Case-facts block, trimmed tool output. Module: twelve. When to escalate. Best answer: Explicit criteria plus few-shot; honor "get me a person" at once; policy gaps; not sentiment or confidence. Module: thirteen.

1.title: Scenario 1: Customer Support Resolution Agent, continued
1.text: Scenario one: Customer Support Resolution Agent, continued. Handoff. Best answer: Structured summary (customer, root cause, amount, recommended action). Module: three. Traps: "stronger prompt" for a hard rule; a classifier before criteria; picking one of several customer matches by heuristic. Exam tip: Support-agent items usually test enforcement (gates and hooks), tool descriptions, escalation criteria and structured errors.

1.title: Scenario 2: Code Generation with Claude Code
1.text: Scenario two: Code Generation with Claude Code. Requirement: a team uses Claude Code for generation, refactoring, debugging and docs; custom slash commands, Claude dot M D, plan mode versus direct execution.

1.title: Scenario 2: Code Generation with Claude Code, continued
1.text: Scenario two: Code Generation with Claude Code, continued. Team standards. Best answer: Project Claude dot M D, not user-level. Module: seven. Shared command. Best answer: the dot Claude commands folder in the repository. Module: seven. Conventions for files spread everywhere (tests). Best answer: Path-specific rules with glob patterns. Module: seven. Large restructuring. Best answer: Plan mode, then direct execution. Module: eight. One-file fix with a stack trace. Best answer: Direct execution. Module: eight. Verbose exploration. Best answer: Explore subagent; skill with context: fork. Module: seven, eight. Long sessions degrade. Best answer: Scratchpad, subagents, slash compact. Module: twelve. Inconsistent results from prose. Best answer: two to three input or output examples; tests first; interview. Module: eight.

1.title: Scenario 2: Code Generation with Claude Code, continued
1.text: Scenario two: Code Generation with Claude Code, continued. Traps: one giant root Claude dot M D; per-directory Claude dot M D files for scattered tests; "start direct and switch if it gets hard".

1.title: Scenario 3: Multi-Agent Research System
1.text: Scenario three: Multi-Agent Research System. Requirement: a coordinator delegates to web-search, document-analysis, synthesis and report subagents; cited, comprehensive reports. Architecture. Best answer: Hub-and-spoke; all communication through the coordinator. Module: two. Incomplete coverage though subagents succeeded. Best answer: Fix the coordinator's decomposition. Module: two. Passing context. Best answer: Put findings and metadata in the subagent prompt (no inheritance). Module: two. Parallelism. Best answer: Several Task calls in one response. Module: two. Tool scope. Best answer: Role-specific tools; scoped verify fact for synthesis. Module: six. Timeouts. Best answer: Structured error context, partial results, coverage annotations. Module: thirteen. Attribution and conflicts. Best answer: Claim-source mappings, both values with dates. Module: fourteen. Context budgets. Best answer: Upstream agents return structured facts, not long text. Module: twelve.

1.title: Scenario 3: Multi-Agent Research System, continued
1.text: Scenario three: Multi-Agent Research System, continued. Traps: blaming downstream agents; suppressing a failure as an empty success; aborting the whole run; averaging conflicting statistics. Exam tip: Research-system items usually test coordinator decomposition, context passing, error context and provenance.

1.title: Scenario 4: Developer Productivity with Claude
1.text: Scenario four: Developer Productivity with Claude. Requirement: an S D K agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar code, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate chores with Read, Write, Bash, Grep and Glob plus M C P servers.

1.title: Scenario 4: Developer Productivity with Claude, continued
1.text: Scenario four: Developer Productivity with Claude, continued. Find callers of a function. Best answer: Grep the name, then Read to follow flow. Module: six. Find files by pattern. Best answer: Glob. Module: six. Edit fails (non-unique text). Best answer: Read plus Write. Module: six. Shared integrations. Best answer: Project dot M C P dot Jason with the env variable tokens; community servers for standard tools. Module: six. Agent prefers Grep over a better M C P tool. Best answer: Rich M C P tool description. Module: six. Reduce exploratory calls. Best answer: M C P resources (catalogs). Module: six. Resuming work. Best answer: Named session; tell it which files changed; fresh summary if stale. Module: four. Traps: reading the whole repository up front; building a custom server for a standard integration.

1.title: Scenario 5: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
1.text: Scenario five: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Requirement: automated code review, test generation and P R (pull request) feedback; actionable comments with few false positives. Non-interactive run. Best answer: dash p. Module: eight. Machine-readable findings. Best answer: dash dash output format json plus dash dash json schema. Module: eight. Project context for C I. Best answer: Claude dot M D (standards, fixtures, criteria). Module: eight. False positives. Best answer: Explicit report or skip criteria; disable a noisy category temporarily; severity examples. Module: nine. Format consistency. Best answer: Few-shot with location, issue, severity, fix. Module: nine. Duplicate comments after new commits. Best answer: Pass prior findings; report only new. Module: eight. Big pull request. Best answer: Per-file passes plus integration pass. Module: four, eleven. Reviewing generated code. Best answer: Independent instance. Module: eight, eleven. Cost saving. Best answer: Batch only non-blocking jobs. Module: eleven.

1.title: Scenario 5: Claude Code for Continuous Integration, continued
1.text: Scenario five: Claude Code for Continuous Integration, continued. Traps: a confidence cutoff for precision; batch for pre-merge checks; asking the same session to double-check.

1.title: Scenario 6: Structured Data Extraction
1.text: Scenario six: Structured Data Extraction. Requirement: extract fields from unstructured documents, validate with Jason (Java Script Object Notation) schemas, keep accuracy high, handle edge cases, feed downstream systems.

1.title: Scenario 6: Structured Data Extraction, continued
1.text: Scenario six: Structured Data Extraction, continued. Guaranteed structure. Best answer: Tool use plus Jason schema. Module: ten. Unknown document type. Best answer: tool choice: "any" with several schemas. Module: six, ten. Missing data. Best answer: Nullable fields (no fabrication); unclear, other plus detail. Module: ten. Semantic errors. Best answer: Validation code; calculated total versus stated total; conflict detected. Module: ten. Retry. Best answer: With document plus failed output plus errors; not when the info is absent. Module: ten. Bulk processing. Best answer: Batches A P I (application programming interface) with custom id; resubmit failures; tune on a sample. Module: eleven. Quality at scale. Best answer: Per-type and per-field accuracy; stratified sampling; calibrated confidence. Module: fourteen. Varied formats. Best answer: Few-shot with different structures. Module: nine.

1.title: Scenario 6: Structured Data Extraction, continued
1.text: Scenario six: Structured Data Extraction, continued. Traps: trusting ninety-seven percent overall accuracy; retrying on absent data; required fields that force invention. Exam tip: Extraction items usually test tool use with schemas, nullable fields, retry limits, batches and accuracy by segment.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. one Support agent: Gate plus hook for hard rules; descriptions; structured errors; case facts; criteria plus few-shot escalation; structured handoff. two Claude Code: Project Claude dot M D; commands in repo; path rules; plan versus direct; fork or Explore. three Multi-agent research: Hub-and-spoke; decomposition; context in prompts; scoped tools; error context; provenance. four Developer productivity: Grep to Read; Glob; Read plus Write; dot M C P dot Jason; M C P resources; sessions. five C I: dash p; Jason schema output; Claude dot M D; explicit criteria; few-shot; per-file plus integration; independent review; batch non-blocking only. six Extraction: Tool use plus schema; nullable; validation plus retry; batches; segment accuracy; calibrated confidence.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. (Support agent) Production data shows the agent sometimes issues a refund before checking that the customer owns the order. Which change gives the strongest guarantee? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A hard business requirement needs a deterministic gate; the other options reduce but do not remove the failure rate.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. (Claude Code) Engineers disagree on style because the team's conventions live in one engineer's home-directory configuration. What fixes the root cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. User-level configuration is personal; project-level files are shared through version control.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. (Research system) A subagent succeeds, but the final report lacks citations, because the synthesis subagent received only the instruction to combine findings. What fixes it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Subagents do not inherit context; attribution must travel in the prompt.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. (Developer productivity) The agent must locate every use of apply Discount and then understand how it is called. What sequence is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Grep finds content; Read follows the flow; Glob matches names, not contents.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. (C I) A review bot produces many low-value comments about naming, and developers have stopped reading it. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Categorical criteria and temporarily disabling a noisy category restore trust.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. (Extraction) A pipeline reports ninety-eight percent accuracy overall, but receipts from one retailer are mostly wrong. What should the team do before reducing human review? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Aggregate accuracy hides weak segments; validate per segment and keep sampling.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: C. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: A. Question five: C. Question six: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
